core: Working definition of global health (Koplan et al., The Lancet, 2009): an area for study, research, and practice prioritizing improving health and achieving equity in health for all people worldwide
Scope distinction: global vs international vs public health (cross-border problems vs one country helping another vs within-country population health)
The players: WHO, UNICEF, national agencies, NGOs
The issues: infectious disease, noncommunicable disease, health systems, maternal and child health
The equity lens: global health targets the world's biggest health gaps
How cooperation works: surveillance, funding, guidelines, research
Honest framing: global health as the world's shared waiting room

CDC Global Health Center framing ('a disease threat anywhere is a disease threat everywhere') and its country-office work

claims.claim: The most commonly cited working definition of global health — 'an area for study, research, and practice that places a priority on improving health and achieving equity in health for all people worldwide' — was written by Jeffrey Koplan and colleagues with the executive board of the Consortium of Universities for Global Health and published as a viewpoint in The Lancet in 2009.

Global health emphasizes transnational health issues, determinants, and solutions; involves many disciplines beyond the health sciences; and is a synthesis of population-based prevention with individual-level clinical care.

Global health differs from public health in scope, governance, and complexity: it targets health issues prioritized at international or global levels rather than local or national scales, and its decision-making involves a more diverse set of multilateral and multisectoral actors than public health.

Global health was established as a distinct field in the late 1990s with the goal of replacing older, often colonial models of international health engagement with more equitable partnerships, and it brought a broader array of funders, new public–private partnerships, and expanded roles for governments, businesses, and civil society organizations.

The World Health Organization, founded in 1948, is the United Nations agency that connects nations, partners and people to promote health, keep the world safe and serve the vulnerable; it leads global efforts to expand universal health coverage and directs and coordinates the world's response to health emergencies.

The CDC's Global Health Center states that 'a disease threat anywhere is a disease threat everywhere' and works on threats including COVID-19, vaccine-preventable diseases, HIV, TB, and malaria; CDC country offices support partner countries in surveillance, laboratory, emergency management, and workforce development.

Noncommunicable diseases (heart disease, cancer, chronic respiratory disease, diabetes) killed at least 43 million people in 2021, about 75% of non-pandemic-related deaths globally, and 73% of all NCD deaths occur in low- and middle-income countries.
UNICEF works in more than 190 countries and territories to protect the rights of every child, which places child health, nutrition, and immunization at the center of its mandate.
The WHO Constitution declares that the enjoyment of the highest attainable standard of health is one of the fundamental rights of every human being.

Immunization is a cornerstone global health program: the WHO tracks immunization coverage worldwide and issues guidance on vaccines, and coverage gaps between countries are a standard illustration of the equity lens.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether global health is a distinct field or simply public health practiced at a larger scale.
positions: Some writers treat global health as public health applied worldwide, with no meaningful boundary.

Koplan et al. (2009) and later literature argue global health differs in scope, governance, and complexity: transnational issues and a more diverse set of multilateral and multisectoral actors than public health.
The 2025 updated-definition literature argues the 2009 definition should itself be revised to make One Health and sustainability visible.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson follows the Koplan framing: global health concerns transnational problems and international cooperation, while public health is the within-country population-health field (a sibling topic). The lesson notes the field is still debating updates to its definition without taking sides.

conflictingEvidence.issue: NCD burden figures vary by vintage and by what is counted as 'non-pandemic-related' deaths.
positions: Older WHO fact-sheet figures cited 41 million NCD deaths (74% of all deaths).
The current WHO fact sheet (updated 25 September 2025) cites at least 43 million NCD deaths in 2021, 75% of non-pandemic-related deaths.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the current WHO figures with the 2021 vintage stated, and avoids comparing vintages.

sourceRecords.title: Towards a common definition of global health
sourceRecords.provider: The Lancet (Koplan JP, Bond TC, Merson MH, et al.)
sourceRecords.notes: Metadata (authors, journal, volume 373, pages 1993-1995, 2009) verified via Crossref DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(09)60332-9; full-text is paywalled, so the definition wording and the public-health/global-health distinction were verified through verbatim quotation in the open-access 2025 paper (updated-definition-global-health-2025). Source of the working definition and the 'transnational health issues, determinants, and solutions' framing.
